newsitem.title: USA: MAC weighs $1.8 bln New York City financing plan.
newsitem.headline: MAC weighs $1.8 bln New York City financing plan.

text.p: The Municipal Assistance Corp (MAC) for the New York City on Wednesday said it was considering a $1.8 billion financing plan that would provide New York City with about $250 million over the next 17 months.
The board of the MAC, set up in the mid-1970s to rescue the city from a fiscal crisis, will meet on Thursday to consider approving a total of $1.4 billion of bond sales.
The financing would be broken down into a series of refundings, according to a prepared statement.
The first sale of fixed-rate bonds, set for February 26, would total about $494.7 million. The underwriters would be led by Morgan Stanley.
A second sale of $492.4 million of fixed-rate bonds in April would be led by J.P. Morgan Securities.
Smith Barney would lead the syndicate for a third offering of $405 million of variable rate bonds, scheduled for April or May.
Goldman Sachs will run the books for a $390.9 million sale of fixed-rate bonds planned for October, the MAC said.

In April 1998, the MAC would sell $230 million of fixed-rate bonds under the plan. In April 1999, it expected to offer $200 million of fixed-rate bonds. The leaders of the syndicates for those two sales have not yet been selected.
After 17 months, the MAC's financial plan was expected to save the city about $13 million each year until 2008.
Edward Regan, chairman of the MAC, warned the administration of New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani not to fritter away the windfall, which Regan said belonged to the taxpayers.
"How the savings are used should be determined by the city's elected officials," he said in prepared remarks.

"The availability of these savings is subject to only one restriction -- as a one-time resource, they should be applied to one-time expenditures. In other words, they should not contribute to the city's structural deficit."
